episodes.title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
episodes.description:
Vector search can't answer "which PRs did I merge last week?" A relational context engine can, and it cuts token burn along the way.

Peter Werry, founding engineer at Unblocked, explains what a context engine is and why coding agents need more than code search: the PRs, Slack threads and incident history that explain why the code is the way it is. He shows Claude sessions with and without that context, including one with about a 50% drop in cost and one that traced a regression to a model switch. Then he builds Unblocked's open-source document query engine step by step: automatic schema discovery, identity resolution across systems, query validation that blocks dangerous operators, retries that feed errors back to the model, and full-text search. He closes with the open-source context engine simulator for testing whether pre-gathered context helps your agents.

In this talk:
• What a context engine is, and how it lowers cost on real agent sessions
• Why vector stores can't answer structural questions about your work
• Turning plain-English questions into safe, validated database queries
• Schema discovery, identity resolution, retries and full-text search

episodes.title: Zero Cold Starts: Serverless AI Agents on Akamai Functions — Thorsten Hans
episodes.description:
Cold starts, proprietary SDKs and one-region deployments slow AI apps down. WebAssembly at the edge removes all three.

Thorsten Hans, senior developer advocate at Akamai, shows how to build and ship MCP servers and AI agents with Spin, the open-source WebAssembly framework, and run them on Akamai Functions, a globally distributed serverless platform with no cold starts. He explains why WebAssembly on the server is fast, portable and sandboxed by default, then live-codes MCP servers with wasmcp: scaffolding tools in TypeScript and Rust, composing them into a full server, testing with MCP Inspector, deploying it worldwide in about 60 seconds with one command, and calling its tools from the Zed editor. He finishes with an agent built on the Vercel AI SDK, backed by a model on a Linode GPU, and explains how memory snapshots keep apps warm.

In this talk:
• Why edge-native beats single-region for AI apps, and how WebAssembly kills cold starts
• What Spin and Akamai Functions are
• Building and composing MCP servers with wasmcp in TypeScript and Rust
• Deploying an MCP server and an AI agent globally with one command

episodes.title: From Your Laptop to the Pipeline: Scaling Custom Agents with GitHub Copilot
episodes.description:
Most teams build an agent once, on one laptop, and never share it. Here's how to take it from local to the whole org to the CI pipeline.

Jose Palafox, who has spent six and a half years at GitHub and now works with companies on Copilot adoption, walks through the path from a local custom agent to agents that run unattended in your pipeline. He explains how Copilot works under the hood, the built-in agents in the Copilot CLI, and how to generate and edit a custom agent with the agent builder. Then he shows how to share agents across an organization with a marketplace, run agents across repositories with Orchestrate, and move them into CI with GitHub Agentic Workflows: headless Copilot CLI runs in GitHub Actions, triggered by slash commands in issues, plus a repo with about 200 agents running different parts of the pipeline and agents that investigate their own cost overruns.

In this talk:
• Local vs autonomous agents, and how Copilot works under the hood
• Building custom agents and choosing models for them
• Sharing agents across a company with a marketplace
• Running agents in CI with GitHub Agentic Workflows

episodes.title: The Lethal Trifecta Is Already on Your Laptops — Michael Patterson, Coder
episodes.description:
Your coding agent can read private data, take in untrusted content and talk to the internet. That's the lethal trifecta, and it's already running on your developers' laptops.

Michael Patterson, staff solutions engineer at Coder, explains Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally) and why agents like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw running on a laptop hit all three. He covers prompt injection, what blocks big companies from rolling out agents (CISO concerns, shadow AI on personal subscriptions, alert fatigue, skeptical senior engineers), and three architectural guardrails: cloud development environments that isolate the agent, a model proxy that logs traffic and strips sensitive data before it reaches the LLM provider, and an agent firewall that denies commands and domains you didn't allow.

In this talk:
• What the lethal trifecta is, and why laptop agents hit all three parts
• How prompt injection turns trusted sources into attacks
• What security teams worry about when agents roll out at scale
• Three guardrails: cloud dev environments, a model proxy and an agent firewall

episodes.title: From 15% to 90% GPU Utilization: Fix the Data Pipeline, Not the Model
episodes.description:
Your GPUs might be waiting on your data, not your model. This pipeline went from 15% to 90% GPU utilization.

Tarun Sunkaraneni from Amazon AGI shows that the hardest part of fast multimodal training often isn't the GPU at all, but keeping it fed with data. Training a Qwen3-VL-style model on images stored in S3, the baseline pipeline spent about 85% of its time waiting on data, mostly loading, decoding and resizing images one at a time. He fixes the bottlenecks one by one: concurrency with asyncio and Ray actors, prefetching so data is ready before the trainer asks, and Ray's object store to stop copying big image tensors between processes. Then, at production scale, a new bottleneck appears on a single machine's network card, solved by spreading workers across nodes and using zero-copy reads, which gave another 50% throughput.

In this talk:
• Why multimodal training is often CPU- and IO-bound, not GPU-bound
• Concurrency, prefetching and zero-copy transfer with Ray
• Choosing between asyncio, threads and processes around the GIL
• Why some settings only pay off at scale

episodes.title: Small Models, Big Results: Training a Finance Agent for Under $500 — Charles Dickens, Snorkel AI
episodes.description:
A 4 billion parameter model, trained with RL for under $500, beat its 235 billion parameter sibling on real financial questions.

Charles Dickens, research scientist at Snorkel AI, shares how Snorkel and UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab trained a small model to beat a much bigger one. Working from SEC 10-K filings, they built FinQA, a financial question-answering dataset with expert-validated answers, and found even frontier models hallucinating table schemas, flooding their own context, and repeating failed strategies. Using the open-source rLLM framework and reinforcement learning with a simple pass/fail reward, they trained a Qwen3 4B model for under $500 that reached about 60% versus 51% for the 235B model. The skills transferred to harder multi-table questions without hurting general tool use. Surprisingly, simpler training data and simpler rewards worked best, because the real bottleneck was disciplined tool use, not reasoning depth.

In this talk:
• How the FinQA dataset was built and verified from 10-K filings
• Failure modes: hallucinated schemas, context flooding, poor recovery
• Training a 4B model with RL in rLLM for under $500
• Why simple data and binary rewards beat fancier setups

episodes.title: Why Your Company Needs a Context Graph (and How to Build It) — Gil Feig, Merge
episodes.description:
Your agent can tell you why one customer was upset. Ask which customers were upset last year, and it falls apart.

Gil Feig, co-founder and CTO of Merge, explains why every company needs a context graph, a company brain that brings together third-party data, structured context, memories and skills. Using the question "which customers were upset last week?", he shows why connecting a few MCP servers isn't enough: live API lookups can't search across large datasets, so you need a synced copy for semantic queries, alongside live calls for simple lookups. He walks through the architecture: a router, synced and live context, a summarizer, and skills and memory that encode how your company actually defines things like a happy customer. He covers four tiers of context including derived summaries, a decision flowchart for when to use cache or live data, and why every answer must keep track of where its data came from.

In this talk:
• Why MCP live lookups can't answer questions across large datasets
• Combining synced data, live lookups, a router and a summarizer
• Why company skills and memory belong in the context layer
• Traceability: where data came from, when, and what invalidates it

episodes.title: Generation Is Cheap, Review Is Expensive: How to Stop Shipping AI Slop — Gabriel Martinez, G2i
episodes.description:
Slop isn't AI-written code. It's work that looks finished before the thinking is.

Gabriel "Gabo" Martinez, engineering manager and self-described slop warden at G2i, explains what slop really is: what happens when generation outruns judgment, when ambiguity gets cleared with guesses and nobody notices there was a choice to make. He's not anti-AI, but argues we need to sober up. Code is still a liability, agents make a messy codebase messier faster, and quick prototypes convince stakeholders the hard part is done. He covers the pressure to merge faster than you can review, thousand-line PRs, 20-page AI docs that push the thinking onto reviewers, and why generation is cheap but evaluation is expensive. His fixes are conventions, diagrams as the review surface, small reviewable changes and clear ownership, inspired by Rails, plus why G2i built ORC.

In this talk:
• What slop is, and why it's about missing judgment, not AI
• Why code is a liability and AI makes the ball of mud bigger
• Incentives that push teams to merge faster than they can review
• Conventions, diagrams and small changes that keep humans in control

episodes.title: From Context to Memory: Your Agents Need a Real Memory Layer — Anders Swanson, Oracle
episodes.description:
Your agent rereads the same files every session because nothing it learned was saved.

Anders Swanson, developer evangelist for Oracle Database, treats agent memory as a systems problem. Context windows aren't memory, bigger windows aren't the fix, and markdown scratch pads and grep don't scale. Keep going down that road and you'll end up building your own database. He walks through the pattern modern memory systems are converging on: formation, recall, evolution and evaluation, plus governance. That means typed memories (episodic, semantic, procedural and working state), a storage schema with vectors, text indexes, graph links, time and audit history, redaction before anything is written, and hybrid search that blends several retrieval methods. He covers failure modes like stale, mis-scoped, poisoned and conflicting memories, and why feedback is what closes the loop.

In this talk:
• Why context windows and scratch files aren't memory
• Typed memories and a storage schema built for recall
• Forming memories safely, and recalling them with hybrid search
• Stale, poisoned and conflicting memories, and how feedback fixes them

episodes.title: Designing CLIs for Agents, Not Humans — Pedro Lopez, Airbyte
episodes.description:
Airbyte built both an MCP server and a CLI so agents can use its data. Here's what each one is actually good for.

Pedro Lopez, software engineer at Airbyte, shares lessons from building two ways for AI agents to reach company data through Airbyte's Context Store, a search-optimized index of tools like Zendesk, Stripe and HubSpot. Both are thin interfaces over one platform, built from OpenAPI specs. For the MCP server, he explains why to keep the tool count small and use progressive discovery, why OAuth is the only realistic way to sign in, why users expect long-lived sessions, and why URL elicitation isn't ready across clients yet. For the CLI, he explains designing for agents instead of humans: JSON in and JSON out, consistent noun-verb commands, skills that ship with the tool, and no interactive prompts. He closes with when to choose MCP and when to choose a CLI.

In this talk:
• Keeping MCP tool counts small with progressive discovery
• OAuth, long sessions, and elicitation in real MCP clients
• Designing a CLI for agents: JSON in, JSON out, consistency, skills
• When to choose MCP, and when to choose a CLI
